samples.reverse_paraphrase: The numerical-computation ideal is historical; modern computers' symbol manipulation is mentioned separately before formal models are compared.
A set or k-ary relation is computable when membership of a number or tuple is decidable, via its characteristic function.
Partial recursive functions can be undefined; general recursive functions are the total functions among the partial recursive ones.
Start at h(0), then use the already known h(x) to calculate h(x+1); the source sentence with reversed direction is corrected and disclosed.
For the general primitive-recursion scheme, f gives the base value without h and g uses the parameters, y and only the immediately preceding h-value.
The composite h takes n original arguments; f receives k outputs from the g_i; the source's k-1 left index is corrected to n-1.
Projections let a composition ignore, repeat, or permute arguments and nest an l-place inner composition.
The inductive class starts from zero, successor and all projections, then closes under composition and primitive recursion of the stated arities.
Addition is primitive recursive only after g(x0,y,z)=Succ(z) is represented as Succ(Proj_2^3(x0,y,z)); one-place and three-place functions are not identified.
A dummy argument first adapts a unary recursive example to the stipulated k>=1 scheme; constants and multiplication are built from base functions.
Addition's notation is Rec_1[Proj_0^1, Comp_{1,3}[Succ,Proj_2^3]], with all arity parameters unchanged.
Computing h(x,y) requires finitely many successive evaluations from 0 through y when f and g are computable.
Exponentiation's informal recurrence is converted to formal primitive recursion using a constant-one f and projections inside multiplication g.
Predecessor needs a dummy x argument; its successor clause selects y with Proj_1^3 and need not use the prior predecessor value.
Factorial is formalized using a two-place h with constant-one base and multiplication by successor of y.
Truncated subtraction gives zero when x<y and x-y otherwise; its recurrence applies predecessor after each subtraction step.
Finite sums and finite products are closure operations, and the displayed proof gives the recurrence only for sums.
The non-strict order x<=y is IsZero(x truncated-minus y), so the Gujarati name includes equality.
Bounded universal quantification begins true at y=0 and combines the next relation value by minimum; bounded existential uses maximum or De Morgan duality.
Case-defined primitive recursive functions choose the first applicable R_i, falling back to g_m when none apply.
If a witness already exists below y, retain it; otherwise inspect R at y and return y or y+1. The third case uses input vector x.
The relation x|y means y is a multiple of x; even for x=y=0 a bounded witness exists, though not every witness is bounded.
The next prime can be found by bounded minimization up to factorial(x)+1 using Euclid's result, hence the prime enumerator is primitive recursive.
Adding one to each exponent makes a trailing zero change the sequence code; zero is selected as the empty-sequence code.
The unique largest prime divisor p_i of a valid nonempty sequence code identifies its final position i and length i+1.
The ith element is the least a for which p_i^(a+2) fails to divide the code, with zero returned past the length.
The sequence-code upper bound is stated for k>=1; the adjacent note gives value 1 for k=0 so the empty code is below it.
A tree code begins with the count of immediate subtrees, then their codes and an optional node label; the two-child example retains its nested tuple.
The helper concatenates f applied to the first k elements, starting with an empty sequence; the subtree accumulator retains levels through n rather than just level n.
Simultaneous recursion updates two functions together, while course-of-values recursion may inspect the full history of earlier values.
Changing side parameters along a recursion is another scheme simulated by ordinary primitive recursion, with no detailed derivation supplied.
Given effective evaluation of an enumeration f_x, h(x)=f_x(x)+1 is computable but differs from each enumerated unary primitive recursive function on its own index.
Successive g_n grow quickly; the Ackermann–Péter diagonal G(x)=g_x(x) outgrows every primitive recursive function.
Recursive notation coding enumerates unary primitive recursive functions, assigning a constant zero function to numbers that do not code a suitable notation.
The diagonal argument applies to any enumerable total class whose indexed evaluation is computable, motivating the addition of partial functions.
Weak equality means both undefined or both equal and defined; composition is defined only when all inner terms and the outer value are defined.
Unbounded minimization finds the least zero only if all earlier partial computations terminate; otherwise the result remains undefined.
Recursive functions are exactly the total members of the partial recursive class.
The unary normal-form equation uses primitive recursive T and U and a single µ-search for a program index e.
T checks a coded computation from input x and index e; U extracts its resulting value from the code s.
The halting characteristic function returns 1 for defined indexed computations and 0 for undefined or invalid indices.
Assuming halting were partial recursive would give a diagonal d whose definedness at its own index contradicts the halting answer.
A regular total function has some zero for every fixed tuple of side parameters, making its µ-search total.
The apparently narrower general-recursive definition and the total partial-recursive definition have the same extension.
